title: Equality and equity: what is the difference?
examples: What is the difference between equality and equity?
Is treating everyone the same always fair?

points: Fair if all start the same

figure.verdict: Both aim at fairness in different ways

explain.say: Three children want to watch a cricket match over a fence, but they are different heights. You have three boxes. Do you give one box each, or share them out by need? Look at the board: two ideas of fairness, side by side.

draw.text: Equality and equity: what is the difference?

left.title: Equality
points: Fair if all start the same

draw.verdict: Both aim at fairness in different ways

explain.say: See the left side, equality? Equality means everyone gets exactly the same: one box each. It is simple and clear, and it is fair when everyone starts in the same place. Can you think of something that should be the same for all?

draw.name: x-compare

left.title: Equality
points: Fair if all start the same

draw.verdict: Both aim at fairness in different ways

explain.say: Now look at the bars. The tall child needs almost no help, the middle child needs about 20 centimetres, and the small child needs about 40. With one box each, the small child still cannot see. Which child do you think needs more help?

items.label: Small child
items.ask: Why does the small child need more help?

explain.say: Look at the right side, equity. Equity means each person gets what they need to reach a fair result. Here the small child gets two boxes and the tall child none, so all three can see. Glasses for a child who cannot see the board is equity too.

left.title: Equality
points: Fair if all start the same

draw.verdict: Both aim at fairness in different ways

explain.say: People debate when to use each. Some say treating everyone the same is fairest; others say we must fix uneven starts. Most systems mix both, like equal votes but extra help for those who need it. Well done! Challenge: find one example of each idea at your school.

faq.a: Equality means treating everyone the same and giving everyone the same things or chances, like one vote per adult or the same rules for all.
Equity means giving each person what they need so they can reach a fair result. People who start further behind get more support, like a ramp for a wheelchair user.

faq.q: Why does the small child need more help?
faq.a: The small child starts further behind, about 40 centimetres too short to see. Giving everyone the same help still leaves them out, so they need extra support to catch up.
asks: Tell me about the small child

faq.a: It depends on the situation, and people disagree. Equality is fairest when everyone starts equal, such as votes. Equity helps when starts are uneven, such as extra lessons. Many fair systems use both.
asks: Which is better, equality or equity?

faq.a: Glasses for a child who cannot see well, ramps and lifts for wheelchair users, free school meals for families with less money, and extra time in exams for some learning differences.
asks: Give me an example of equity

facts: The fence-and-boxes picture of equality and equity is often credited to Craig Froehle, who drew a version in 2012.
Article 1 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948) says all humans are born free and equal in dignity and rights.

quiz.say: A teacher gives every pupil the same textbook. Is that equality or equity?
quiz.show: Same textbook for every pupil is…
quiz.why: Everyone receives exactly the same thing, which is equality.

wrong.1: Equity would give each pupil what they need, such as a large-print book for a pupil with low vision.
wrong.2: It is a clear case of treating everyone the same.

quiz.say: A school builds a ramp for a pupil who uses a wheelchair. Which idea is this?
quiz.show: Building a ramp for one pupil is…
quiz.why: The ramp gives one pupil what they need to get in, like everyone else: that is equity.

wrong.0: Equality would give everyone the same, but stairs alone leave this pupil out.
wrong.1: It removes a barrier so the pupil has the same chance, which makes things fairer.
